title: Fewest Squares That Add Up to N
statement: A **perfect square** is a number like `1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ...` (the square of a whole number). Given a positive whole number `n`, return the **smallest number of perfect squares** (the same square may be used several times) that add up to exactly `n`.

examples.explanation: 7 = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1. There is no way with fewer squares.

expected.time: O(n * sqrt(n)) with a table, O(sqrt(n)) with number theory

hints.nudge: Whatever the best answer for n is, its LAST square is some i * i. After removing it you are left with a smaller number. What does that remind you of?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over the total: best[m] = 1 + min(best[m - i * i]) over all squares i * i <= m. (There is also a very short answer from number theory: it is never more than 4.)
hints.walkthrough: A greedy 'take the biggest square first' fails (12 = 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 needs 4 squares, but 12 = 4 + 4 + 4 needs 3), and plain recursion repeats work. Build a table: best[m] is the fewest squares for the total m. For any total m, one of the squares in an optimal sum is some i * i, and the rest add up to m - i * i, which has its own best value, so best[m] = 1 + the smallest best[m - i * i] over all squares not larger than m. The table needs n entries with about sqrt(n) choices each: O(n sqrt(n)), fine for n = 10000. A faster way uses two theorems: every number is a sum of at most four squares; it needs exactly 4 only when, after dividing out all factors of 4, it leaves remainder 7 when divided by 8; otherwise check 1 (n is a square), then 2 (n - i * i is a square for some i), else 3.
